newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean strike leaders plot future strategy.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean strike leaders plot future strategy.

text.p: South Korean union leaders on Saturday plotted new strategies to pressure the government into making further concessions on a controversial labour law.

A spokesman of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions said the leaders gathered at a Seoul office to deliberate future steps after abandoning their tent headquarters at Myongdong Cathedral on Friday.
"We left the cathedral to avoid further inconvenience to the church. Our struggle will continue until the vicious law is made void and a new law is in place," Chung Sung-hee told Reuters.
The law adopted in December makes it easier for companies to sack workers and replace strikers, and bans the confederation until the year 2000.
"A new agenda will be adopted in the Central Committee meeting on Tuesday," he said.

The confederation, which has led work stoppages since the law was rammed through parliament on December 26, has vowed to organise the "biggest ever rally by workers" on Sunday to mark the one-month anniversary of its campaign.
From this week, the confederation has limited strikes to once a week on Wednesdays.

Chung accused political parties of insincerity in trying to seek a compromise over the labour law. The main opposition National Congress for New Politics on Friday softened its stand and said it was prepared to debate the law in parliament if the government apologised for its forced passage.
The party had previously said it and a smaller opposition party would hold dialogue with the government only if the legislation were first revoked.
"Political parties have failed to produce any timetable for a revision of the law," Chung said. "After the law is scrapped, a new law should be written before March 1."

President Kim Young-sam made a dramatic concession on Tuesday by agreeing to reopen parliamentary debate on the law and criticising his ruling New Korea Party for not recognising the confederation immediately.
He also ordered the suspension of arrest warrants against confederation president Kwon Young-kil and other strike leaders, paving the way for their leaving Myongdong Cathedral.
The president had previously ruled out a revision or compromise and said dumping the law would be unconstitutional.
Kwon on Saturday made a new demand that companies pay wages to strikers as their protests stemmed from the forced passage of the labour law.
South Korea's economy, which has lost more than three billion dollars from the stoppages, faced a fresh blow as the country's second biggest steel maker faced collapse due to financial problems.

Hanbo Steel Corp, flagship of South Korea's 14th largest industrial conglomerate, defaulted on debt payments on Thursday and was seeking court receivership that would allow it to freeze payments on debt totaling 5.7 trillion won ($6.7 billion).
Analysts said its collapse could spark a chain reaction of corporate bankruptcies and threaten banks.
Hanbo's crisis was caused largely by plant expansion, not the strikes. But it sent shivers through unions, who believe that troubled companies will trim costs through staff cuts.
